Well, it's not, because I think Scripture is a story, and it's a story with a beginning and a middle and an end and development and a fall and lots of twists and turns along the way. And that's not really, I hope it doesn't come across as that's the post-hoc rationalisation for, oh, I don't like the Old Testament. I do like the Old Testament. I read the Old Testament every day.
But Jesus himself told us to read the Bible in a certain way. So in Matthew chapter 19, he's asked a particularly thorny ethical dilemma from his own day. And it actually gives a framework to tell the story of scripture. He said, well, in the beginning, it was like this.
But then there was a fall and our hearts were hardened, so Moses told the people this, that this was a non-ideal set of affairs. And there are many things in the Old Testament that are profoundly non-ideal, right?
And then Jesus says, and I have come to restore things to the intention at the beginning. So there's lots we could go into there, but I think it's very important to read scripture as a story with a shape to it.
In the beginning, goodness, a fall into something that's very suboptimal. And even Jesus says, look, Moses gave you even laws that were suboptimal. How much more suboptimal was the behaviour of the people to whom those laws were given? And even within the Old Testament, there's lots of questioning of.
of the activity of the people and and all that kind of thing. So that's that's that's the way a Christian reads scripture through the lens of Jesus as we see the shape of the story. I think this is a really key question because obviously you're articulating that Christianity is the best, goodness, bestest thing that's ever evolved in the world.
